subject: ela
intro: This quiz checks how well you can identify and explain point of view in a literary text. Each question includes the short passage or poem it is about. Read carefully, then choose the single best answer.

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'I pressed my face to the cold window and counted the cars below, hoping my brother would finally come home.'

From whose point of view is this passage told?

A) First person, because the narrator uses 'I' and 'my' and shares only his or her own thoughts
B) Third person limited, because the narrator describes the brother
C) Third person omniscient, because the narrator knows everyone's thoughts
D) Second person, because the passage speaks directly to the reader
items.answer: A) First person, because the narrator uses 'I' and 'my' and shares only his or her own thoughts

steps: Look for pronouns that signal who is telling the story. The words 'I,' 'my,' and 'me' mark a first person narrator.
The narrator shares only his or her own thoughts and feelings ('hoping my brother would finally come home'), which is typical of first person.
B is wrong because point of view depends on who is telling the story and which pronouns are used, not on who the story describes; the 'I' makes this first person.
C is wrong because the narrator reveals no one's thoughts but his or her own, so it cannot be omniscient.
D is wrong because the passage never addresses the reader as 'you.'
solution.answer: A) First person, because the narrator uses 'I' and 'my' and shares only his or her own thoughts

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'Marco zipped his jacket and stepped onto the bus. He found a seat near the back and stared out the window. The driver pulled away from the curb.'

From whose point of view is this passage told?

A) First person, because the narrator is a character in the story
B) Third person, because the narrator uses 'he' and names the characters from the outside
C) Second person, because it tells the reader what to do
D) First person, because Marco's name is mentioned
items.answer: B) Third person, because the narrator uses 'he' and names the characters from the outside

steps: Check the pronouns. The narrator uses 'he' and refers to characters by name ('Marco,' 'The driver'), which signals third person.
There is no 'I' or 'we,' so the narrator is not a character telling his own story.
A and D are wrong because a story can name and describe a character like Marco without being told from his first person 'I' point of view; point of view depends on who tells it, not who it is about.
C is wrong because the passage never addresses the reader as 'you.'
solution.answer: B) Third person, because the narrator uses 'he' and names the characters from the outside

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'My cousin called it the trip of a lifetime. Six hours in a hot car listening to him brag about his trophies. Some lifetime.'

What is the narrator's attitude toward the trip?

A) Excited and grateful for the time together
B) Sarcastic and unimpressed, mocking the idea that the trip was special
C) Frightened by the long car ride
D) Calm and neutral, simply describing the trip without any feeling
items.answer: B) Sarcastic and unimpressed, mocking the idea that the trip was special

steps: The narrator repeats the cousin's praise ('trip of a lifetime') and then undercuts it with 'Some lifetime,' a sarcastic echo.
The details ('hot car,' 'brag about his trophies') show annoyance, not enjoyment.
A is wrong because the narrator clearly is not grateful or excited; the tone is mocking.
C is wrong because nothing in the passage shows fear.
D is wrong because the narrator does express a strong attitude; reading it as neutral misses the sarcasm in 'Some lifetime.'
solution.answer: B) Sarcastic and unimpressed, mocking the idea that the trip was special

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'Dana smiled at the gift, but inside she dreaded the long visit ahead. Across the room, her aunt felt the same secret worry, though neither of them said a word. Only the clock seemed honest, ticking out the slow afternoon.'

Is this narrator third person limited or third person omniscient, and how do you know?

A) Third person limited, because the narrator reveals only Dana's thoughts
B) First person, because the narrator seems to know how everyone feels
C) Third person omniscient, because the narrator reveals the private thoughts of more than one character
D) Third person omniscient, because the passage takes place in one room
items.answer: C) Third person omniscient, because the narrator reveals the private thoughts of more than one character

steps: An omniscient narrator can enter more than one character's mind. Here the narrator reveals Dana's hidden dread AND the aunt's 'same secret worry.'
Because two characters' private, unspoken feelings are shown ('neither of them said a word'), the narration is omniscient, not limited.
A is wrong because the narrator does not stay inside only Dana's mind; the aunt's secret worry is also revealed.
B is wrong because there is no 'I' or 'we'; the narrator uses 'she' and 'her,' so it is third person, not first person.
D is wrong because the setting being one room does not determine point of view; access to multiple characters' thoughts does.
solution.answer: C) Third person omniscient, because the narrator reveals the private thoughts of more than one character

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'Sam watched the new student eat lunch alone and decided she must be unfriendly. He turned back to his friends, certain he had her figured out. He did not know she had moved three times that year and was too tired to make small talk.'

How does the point of view shape what the reader knows?

A) The narrator stays close to Sam's limited view, so the reader first shares his mistaken judgment, then learns the truth he cannot see, which builds sympathy for the new student
B) The narrator hides everyone's thoughts, so the reader cannot tell what anyone is feeling
C) The narrator proves that the new student really is unfriendly, just as Sam believes
D) The narrator shows that the author dislikes new students and wants the reader to avoid them
items.answer: A) The narrator stays close to Sam's limited view, so the reader first shares his mistaken judgment, then learns the truth he cannot see, which builds sympathy for the new student

steps: The narration follows Sam's limited perspective ('decided she must be unfriendly,' 'certain he had her figured out'), so the reader first sees only what Sam sees.
Then the narrator adds what Sam 'did not know,' revealing the real reason behind the new student's behavior, which makes the reader feel sympathy for her.
B is wrong because the passage does reveal thoughts (Sam's judgment and the truth about the new student), so it is not hiding everything.
C is wrong because the narrator corrects Sam's judgment rather than confirming it; the student is tired, not unfriendly.
D is wrong because it confuses the narrator with the author; the passage shows a character's mistaken view, not the writer's personal opinion.
solution.answer: A) The narrator stays close to Sam's limited view, so the reader first shares his mistaken judgment, then learns the truth he cannot see, which builds sympathy for the new student

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'We never locked our doors back then. We knew every face on the street, and every face knew ours. When a storm knocked out the power, all of us gathered on the Murphys' porch with candles and stories until the lights came back.'

Which choice best explains the words that develop the narrator's point of view?

A) The narrator uses 'they' and 'them' to describe a distant town the narrator never lived in
B) The repeated 'we' and 'our' show the narrator speaks as an insider remembering a shared past, giving the passage a warm, nostalgic perspective
C) The phrase 'back then' proves the narrator is angry about how the neighborhood has changed
D) The mention of the Murphys shows the story is told from the Murphys' point of view
items.answer: B) The repeated 'we' and 'our' show the narrator speaks as an insider remembering a shared past, giving the passage a warm, nostalgic perspective

steps: Trace the pronouns. 'We,' 'our,' and 'us' appear throughout, showing the narrator belongs to the community being described.
The fond memory ('gathered on the porch with candles and stories') gives the passage a warm, nostalgic tone built by that insider perspective.
A is wrong because the narrator uses 'we' and 'our,' not 'they,' and is part of the place, not distant from it.
C is wrong because 'back then' signals fond remembering, not anger; the details are pleasant, so reading anger adds an emotion the text does not support.
D is wrong because naming the Murphys' porch as a setting does not make the Murphys the narrator; the 'we' narrator is telling the story.
solution.answer: B) The repeated 'we' and 'our' show the narrator speaks as an insider remembering a shared past, giving the passage a warm, nostalgic perspective

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: 'I am the most patient brother in the whole world, and everyone says so. When Lily knocked over my model rocket, I only yelled for ten minutes, which is hardly anything. When she borrowed my markers without asking, I forgave her the very next week. Mom keeps telling me to share, but she does not understand how generous I already am. Honestly, Lily is lucky to have a brother like me.'

How does the author develop the narrator's point of view, and what does it let the reader understand?

A) The author uses a biased first person narrator whose own words ('yelled for ten minutes,' 'forgave her the very next week') reveal he is less patient than he claims, so the reader sees a gap between his view of himself and the truth
B) The author uses an omniscient narrator who fairly reports that the brother is the most patient person in the world
C) The author shows that the narrator is completely reliable, so the reader should agree he is generous and patient
D) The author uses third person narration to describe Lily's feelings about her brother
items.answer: A) The author uses a biased first person narrator whose own words ('yelled for ten minutes,' 'forgave her the very next week') reveal he is less patient than he claims, so the reader sees a gap between his view of himself and the truth

steps: The narrator uses 'I' and praises himself as 'the most patient brother,' but his own examples undercut the claim: yelling 'for ten minutes' and waiting a week to forgive are not patient acts.
The author builds an ironic gap between how the narrator sees himself and what the details actually show, so the reader judges him more honestly than he judges himself.
B is wrong because there is no omniscient narrator; the 'I' makes this a biased first person account, and the praise is the narrator's, not a fair report.
C is wrong because taking the narrator's self-praise at face value misses the irony the author builds; the evidence shows he is not as patient as he says.
D is wrong because the passage is first person from the brother and never enters Lily's mind.
solution.answer: A) The author uses a biased first person narrator whose own words ('yelled for ten minutes,' 'forgave her the very next week') reveal he is less patient than he claims, so the reader sees a gap between his view of himself and the truth

items.prompt:
Read the poem:

'They handed me the smallest oar
and told me I would only row,
but watch the water learn my name
the day I choose where we will go.'

What is the speaker's perspective on being given a small role?

A) The speaker is content to row forever and has no wish to lead
B) The speaker feels underestimated but determined, hinting that he or she will one day lead, shown by 'where we will go'
C) The poem proves that the poet personally rows a boat and dislikes oars
D) The speaker is terrified of the water and wants to leave the boat
items.answer: B) The speaker feels underestimated but determined, hinting that he or she will one day lead, shown by 'where we will go'

steps: The speaker is given 'the smallest oar' and told to 'only row,' which shows others underestimate his or her role.
The word 'but' turns the poem toward confidence: 'watch the water learn my name' and 'the day I choose where we will go' show determination to lead in the future.
A is wrong because 'but' and the image of choosing the course show the speaker does not accept staying a follower.
C is wrong because it confuses the speaker with the poet; the perspective belongs to the voice created in the poem, not the writer's own life.
D is wrong because the poem shows ambition and confidence, not fear; nothing suggests the speaker wants to leave.
solution.answer: B) The speaker feels underestimated but determined, hinting that he or she will one day lead, shown by 'where we will go'
